tagline: Forest curves lead past Potomac communities and Caledon’s old-growth woodland.
intro: In King George County, Route 218 becomes Caledon Road and winds through forest beyond Passapatanzy. Most of the county’s stretch is a Virginia Byway. It passes roads to Potomac beach communities and skirts Caledon Natural Area, with its old-growth forest and bald eagle habitat.
Caledon’s landscape changed status in 1974, when ownership passed to Virginia and a 302-acre portion received National Natural Landmark designation for its oak and tulip poplar forest.

Eastbound from Passapatanzy, the road passes Mustoe, Goby and Osso, then Caledon near Ambar and Hampstead. At Berthaville it joins Route 206 to Owens, then turns south toward US 301. Beyond that junction, Route 218 crosses Upper Machodoc Creek and turns onto Tetotum Road, ending at Route 205.

moments.title: Passapatanzy
moments.text: Passapatanzy, on Route 218 in western King George County, was recorded as a Patawomeck village ruled by Japazaws. In 1613, Japazaws conspired with English captain Samuel Argall, who planned to seize Pocahontas as a hostage in negotiations with Powhatan. Mattaponi and Patawomeck tradition places Pocahontas here with her husband, Kocoum. Their daughter, Ka-Okee, survived in the care of other Patawomeck people after Kocoum’s death, in that tradition. A marker concerning this history stands near the Potomac Creek Bridge on US 1 in Stafford, away from the Route 218 community described here.

moments.title: Fairview Beach
moments.text: Fairview Drive leads north from Route 218 to Fairview Beach on the south bank of the Potomac. The community lies six miles northeast of Passapatanzy. It is one of the river communities reached by roads branching north from Caledon Road, alongside Belvedere Beach and Somerset Beach.

moments.title: Caledon
moments.text: Caledon’s protected forest is a specific part of a much larger park: 302 acres within the 2,587-acre Caledon State Park. That portion became a National Natural Landmark in 1974 for its old-growth oak and tulip poplar forest, the same year the property passed to Virginia. The park provides bald eagle habitat along the Potomac. Next door, the privately owned Chotank Creek Natural Area Preserve protects additional eagle habitat and wetlands.
